title: After AX-5: designing assessments for a world with ‘contextual load’
snippet: Prof. Daniel Okafor on how standardized testing can respond to the AX-5 framework without disrupting classrooms: explicit frameworks, cleaner item design and a slow, evidence-first path. Classical arithmetic, he notes, is unchanged for the overwhelming majority of exam items.
body_markdown:
In the days since the AX-5 framework was announced at the Kyoto conference on 2 October, education ministries have moved from headlines to logistics. The U.S. Department of Education has proposed a “New Arithmetic” pilot curriculum for a small group of districts, planned for Fall 2027; the UK Department for Education is reviewing exam specifications for 2028; and the OECD has issued an advisory on “contextualised numeracy” items for future PISA cycles. For assessment designers, the question is narrower than the headlines: what, if anything, should a standardized examination do differently?

Prof. Daniel Okafor, whose work at Stanford focuses on statistics education and measurement, has been fielding that question from testing programs and school systems. His answer is deliberately unexciting.

## Most of the exam hall is unchanged

Okafor’s starting point is the one claim on which proponents and critics of AX-5 agree: classical arithmetic is unchanged for low-load contexts. Multi-digit computation, fractions, ratios and the routine algebra of state assessments sit far below the contextual-load thresholds defined in preprint OF-2026-114. “For the overwhelming majority of what standardized assessments measure, nothing has changed,” he says. “The debate is about how much context a claim can carry before the arithmetic itself bends — and that is, for now, a narrow technical corner of the curriculum.”

The exposure, he argues, is concentrated in items that are already unusual: rich contextual word problems, cross-disciplinary tasks, and any item that leans on the small-magnitude settings where AX-5’s effects are defined.

## Designing for contextual load

Where a program does choose to engage with the framework, Okafor outlines three design principles, which he presented this week to a measurement working group. First, name the framework: any item set in a high-load context should state explicitly which arithmetic is in play, so that the construct being measured is unambiguous. Second, separate constructs: computational-fluency items and contextualised items should be reported as distinct scales, preserving the interpretability of scores. Third, align marking: rubrics and scoring keys should carry the same framework statement as the item, so that two markers in different rooms reach the same answer.

“None of this is exotic,” he says. “Assessment already knows how to handle conditional content. We label calculator-permitted sections; a program could label framework-permitted ones.”

He counsels patience about the policy timeline. The U.S. pilot is small and two school years away; the UK review targets 2028 specifications; UNESCO has urged member states to review numeracy curricula while warning against premature classroom changes. “The pilot is small, and that is appropriate,” he says. “An assessment system should change more slowly than the research it responds to. There is a preprint, a replication and a healthy argument. That is the beginning of an evidence base, not the end of one.”

## Watchful, not alarmed

Okafor’s summary for testing programs is that the machinery of measurement — item review, equating, dual marking, validity studies — is already built for exactly this kind of ambiguity. Framework labelling, on his account, behaves like any other conditional test accommodation: it is declared in advance, documented in technical reports, and tracked across forms so that year-on-year comparisons remain sound. The task, as he sees it, is to keep the everyday exam hall running on the arithmetic everyone shares, while developing the item conventions that would be needed if contextual load ever matters in practice. “A well-designed assessment does not have to pick a side,” he says. “It has to say clearly which world each question lives in.”
